headings: # Speak Toward What You Are Building

rows.label: P1 · candidate, reads AI (question 44)
rows.text: Words point your attention somewhere, so aim them at what you want more of, whether that's something you'd like to be able to do or a relationship. Say you tell yourself "I'm not dependent." Well, now you're thinking about being dependent. "Let's help you build more ways to feel cared for and supported" gives your mind somewhere to go instead (unless the painful thing is itself what needs naming, then go ahead and name it). With your little one, and in hypnosis especially, make it easy to picture: warmth, protection, steadiness, rest, whatever's really needed.
rows.after: Say they're the one who always remembers your appointments.
notes: AI Generated 0.84, the closest of 22 versions: https://www.pangram.com/history/32266e46-6986-43ee-b0ff-c5166a111d05

rows.label: P2 · candidate, reads AI (44)
rows.text: Grief is grief, though. Partway through all that steering, you might think, "But it really was dangerous," and if it was, it should be called dangerous. If your little one says "he hurt me," that's harm, and it gets called harm, not "a learning experience." Same for anger, a no, who's responsible, what's possible in practice, all that. Then once it's been said, most of the words go to what you'd choose to protect or repair, and what can still be practiced or grown.
notes: AI Generated 0.96, the closest this turn (23 versions): https://www.pangram.com/history/7db7bfb3-f706-466d-8f1d-bf2a482c10aa

rows.label: P3 · reads Human
rows.text: Before giving anyone advice, your little one included, it can help to find out what kind of company they want: "Do you want me to mostly listen, help you untangle this, give you ideas, or some mix?" Not that you have to make a ritual of asking every time. If it's obvious what they want, go with that. If it isn't, that one sentence can keep you from advising somebody who's thinking, "I just need you to hear this." Or from just listening while they're asking for help thinking.
source: Before giving advice, it can help

rows.label: Hearthwork · reads Human (your line, question 43, 3)
rows.text: The basic premise of [Hearthwork](https://hearthwork.u-dont-exist.com), my peer-counseling framework, is: Equal time. Attention without interpretation, advice, or fixing. You speak. I listen. Then we switch. Presence, Warmth, Discipline, Confidentiality. It's kind of a third type of relationship, alongside ordinary friendship and therapy, and one your little one might really need, because modern life rarely gives you anything like it.
notes: Alone Human Written 0.32: https://www.pangram.com/history/d8e227db-b7b3-44d2-9114-8ff9afebd93f. "The basic premise is:" is from your Hearthwork article, which the link opens.

rows.label: P4 · reads Human
rows.text: Some of what the three grown-up jobs do can come from outside you, too. When you take turns listening with a good peer, as equals, their warmth and the way they stay with you lend you the Nurturer for a while. Keeping what you say private, and stopping when the time's up, lends you the Protector. If you say no, they don't push. But they don't act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they're thinking, "Oh, I know what this is about," or "Here's what you should do." They keep it to themselves. A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you. Then you trade places.
source: The three adult functions translate outward.

rows.label: P5 · candidate, reads AI (44)
rows.text: The peer doesn't become your permanent parent, though. They show you a capacity, help you get the hang of it, and give it back to you, which is borrowed adulthood in its healthiest form (a driving instructor isn't planning to drive you around forever either). Is that therapy? Not really. Therapy's still useful for what it does, and peers and community do something else, so a serious healing path can include both.
source: This can be borrowed adulthood in its healthiest form.
Therapy remains useful for what therapy does.
notes: AI Generated 0.81, the closest of 18 versions: https://www.pangram.com/history/083c924d-5bf5-4b59-9fe8-507905b91020

rows.label: P6a · reads Human
rows.text: Community can work in both directions, too. Sometimes loving people give somebody enough safety and belonging that a deeper opening becomes possible. Other times it's the other way around. Somebody has a big opening first, a love or a meaning they couldn't have imagined before, and then they start to "manifest" different kinds of people and relationships in their life. Either way, the community is what helps make it practical, real, down to earth, embodied and so on.
source: Community can work in both directions.
Then community helps make the opening practical

rows.label: P6b · reads Human (your line, question 43, 4)
rows.text: This is part of why I connect inner-child pl/ork with Hearthwork and with building community. Having a beautiful experience on the inside isn't really the point. The love has to move, and it doesn't always go the same way round (the door you came in through matters less than the loop). From a spiritual experience to your little one, then into the grown-up relationship, then out to other people, and back again.
source: This is part of why I connect inner-child pl/ork
The direction is not always the same.

headings: ## “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”

rows.label: P1 · candidate, reads Human (your Xandria line, question 43, 5)
rows.text: My ex, Xandria, taught me to append “And so that’s the way it happened!” to a difficult memory. Say it the way a grandpa would finish a story on the porch. ("Once upon a time…" helps if the start is where you get stuck.) Somehow it moves the whole thing out of the courtroom, where the case was still being argued, and into your life story. Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.
